summary: Defines two Mobile IP extensions that let vendors and organizations add their own information to messages for research or deployment. They provide a standard place for custom data. It was replaced by RFC 3115.

eli5.summary: This adds a blank notes field to a form so each company can write its own extra information. A newer document later replaced it.

questions: what are mobile ip vendor extensions
how do vendors add custom data to mobile ip
subtitle: Standardized slots for vendors to add custom data to Mobile IP messages.

tldr.problem: Mobile IP networks needed a way for equipment vendors and organizations to add their own custom information to messages without modifying the core protocol.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3025 defines two new extension types: CVSE (Critical) which must be understood to process a message, and NVSE (Normal) which can be safely ignored if not recognized.
tldr.outcome: This was replaced by RFC 3115, which provided updated vendor extension mechanisms.

today: RFC 3025 was obsoleted by RFC 3115, which provides the current standard for vendor-specific extensions in Mobile IP.

sections.title: Introduction to Vendor Extensions
sections.content:
Mobile IP messages sometimes need to carry vendor-specific or organization-specific information for research, deployment, or proprietary features. Rather than creating entirely new message types, RFC 3025 defines two extension mechanisms that let vendors include custom data in standard Mobile IP messages.

The key idea is graceful degradation: if a receiver does not understand an extension from an unknown vendor, it can either reject the message (for critical extensions) or skip the extension and continue processing (for normal extensions).
sections.eli5: Companies want to add their own custom notes to Mobile IP messages, but without breaking messages for other companies that do not understand those notes.

sections.title: The Two Extension Types
sections.content:
RFC 3025 defines two extension types:

CVSE (Critical Vendor/Organization Specific Extension, Type 37) carries data that is essential to understanding the message. If a receiver recognizes the extension type but does not support the specific vendor ID or vendor type inside it, the entire message MUST be rejected and a registration error returned.

NVSE (Normal Vendor/Organization Specific Extension, Type 133) carries optional vendor data. If a receiver does not recognize the vendor ID or type, it skips the extension but processes the rest of the message normally.

The main structural difference is the length field: CVSE uses 2 octets, NVSE uses 1 octet.
sections.eli5: Critical extensions are like a note that says 'only process this if you understand me.' Normal extensions say 'if you do not understand me, just skip me.' Each has its own type number so routers know which rule to follow.

sections.title: Extension Structure
sections.content:
Both extensions follow a similar structure: a type field, length field, a Vendor/Organization ID (using the SMI (Structure of Management Information) Private Enterprise Code), a vendor-specific type field, and vendor-specific value data.

The Vendor/Org-ID is a 32-bit value where the high-order octet is zero and the low-order 3 octets contain the SMI Private Enterprise Code assigned to the vendor by IANA.

The Vendor-CVSE-Type or Vendor-NVSE-Type field allows each vendor to define its own subtypes within its vendor ID space. The value field holds the actual custom data, which can be zero or more octets.
sections.eli5: Each extension has a header that says who is sending this (the vendor ID), what kind of data it is (the type), and how long the data is. The rest is whatever the vendor wants to include.

sections.title: Processing Rules and Error Handling
sections.content:
When a Mobile IP entity receives a message with a CVSE extension, it checks whether it recognizes both the vendor ID and the vendor-specific type. If it recognizes the extension type itself, but not the specific vendor ID or vendor type, it must reject the registration with a specific error code (100 for Foreign Agent, 140 for Home Agent).

For NVSE extensions, the behavior is more lenient: if the vendor ID or vendor type is not recognized, the entire extension is simply skipped, and processing of the message continues normally.

Multiple extensions of either type can appear in a single message, and they can be placed anywhere after the fixed portion of the message. Each extension should be protected by Mobile IP authentication mechanisms as needed.
sections.eli5: Critical notes must be understood or the whole message is rejected. Normal notes can be ignored without affecting the message. This lets new vendors add features without breaking old systems that do not know about them.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
RFC 3025 assumes that Mobile IP messages are authenticated using the mechanisms defined in the Mobile IP protocol itself. The extension mechanism does not impose additional security requirements; the extensions inherit the security properties of the underlying Mobile IP protocol.

RFC 3025 was obsoleted by RFC 3115 in 2001, which provided updated vendor extension mechanisms that better fit the evolving Mobile IP specification.
sections.eli5: The extensions use the same security checks as the rest of Mobile IP. A newer RFC replaced this one with an improved design.
